en: Dīgha Nikāya 34 Dasuttara Sutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond together with a large Saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks in all.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks:
“Friends, monks!”
“Friends,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“I shall proclaim the Tenfold Series.”
The Dhamma for the attainment of Nibbāna,
for the making of an end of suffering,
and for liberation from all fetters.
1. One Dhamma:
There is one dhamma, friends, that is very helpful; one dhamma to be developed; one dhamma to be fully understood;
one dhamma to be abandoned; one dhamma that leads to decline; one dhamma that leads to distinction; one dhamma that is difficult to penetrate.
One thing is to be brought forth; one thing is to be directly known; one thing is to be realized.
Which one thing is most helpful?
Heedfulness regarding wholesome states.
This one quality is very helpful.
What one quality should be developed?
Mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by a sense of well-being.
This is one dhamma that should be developed.
What is the one dhamma to be fully understood?
Contact that is accompanied by taints and conducive to clinging.
This is one dhamma to be fully understood.
What is the one dhamma to be abandoned?
The conceit "I am."
This is one dhamma to be abandoned.
What is the one dhamma that partakes of decline?
Inappropriate attention.
This is one dhamma that partakes of decline.
What is the one dhamma that partakes of distinction?
Appropriate attention.
This is one quality that partakes of distinction.
What is the one quality that is difficult to penetrate?
It is the immediate concentration of mind.
This is one dhamma that is difficult to penetrate.
What is the one dhamma that should be brought forth?
Unshakable knowledge.
This is one state that should be brought about.
What is the one state to be directly known?
All beings subsist by nutriment.
This is one dhamma to be directly known.
What is the one dhamma to be realized?
Unshakable liberation of mind.
This is one quality to be realized.
Thus, these ten qualities are real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise; they have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
2. Two Qualities.
Two things are very helpful; two things are to be developed; two things are to be fully understood;
two things are to be abandoned; two things lead to decline; two things lead to distinction; two things are difficult to penetrate;
two things are to be generated; two things are to be directly known; two things are to be realized.
Which two things are of great assistance?
Mindfulness and clear comprehension.
These two things are of great assistance.
Which two things are to be developed?
Tranquility and insight.
These two things are to be developed.
Which two things are to be fully understood?
Name and form.
These two things are to be fully understood.
Which two things are to be abandoned?
Ignorance and craving for existence.
These two things are to be abandoned.
Which two things partake of decline?
Refractoriness and association with evil friends.
These two things partake of decline.
Which two things conduce to distinction?
Being easy to speak to and having virtuous friends.
These two things conduce to distinction.
What are the two things that are difficult to penetrate?
That which is the cause and that which is the condition for the defilement of beings; and that which is the cause and that which is the condition for the purification of beings.
These two things are difficult to penetrate.
Which two states are to be developed?
Two kinds of knowledge:
the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
These two things are to be brought forth.
Which two things are to be directly known?
Two elements—
The conditioned element and the unconditioned element.
These two things are to be directly known.
Which two things are to be realized?
Knowledge and liberation—these two things are to be realized.
Thus, these twenty things are real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise; they have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
3. Three Things.
Three things are very helpful; three things are to be developed; … [as before] … three things are to be realized.
What are the three things that are very helpful?
Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—
these three things are very helpful.
What three things are to be developed?
There are three concentrations:

concentration with directed thought and sustained thought; concentration without directed thought and with sustained thought only; and concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought.
These three qualities are to be developed.
Which three things are to be fully understood?
The three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These three things are to be fully understood.
Which three things are to be abandoned?
The three kinds of craving.
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
These three things are to be abandoned.
Which three things partake of decline?
There are three unwholesome roots:
greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root.
These three states lead to decline.
Which three things partake of distinction?
The three roots of the wholesome:
the root of the wholesome that is non-greed, the root of the wholesome that is non-hatred, and the root of the wholesome that is non-delusion.
These three things partake of distinction.
Which three things are difficult to penetrate?
The three elements of escape.

This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely renunciation; this is the escape from forms, namely the formless; and as for whatever has come to be, is conditioned, and is dependently arisen, its cessation is the escape.
These three things are difficult to penetrate.
What are the three things that should be brought forth?
Three kinds of knowledge:
knowledge regarding the past, knowledge regarding the future, and knowledge regarding the present.
These three states are to be developed.
Which three things are to be directly known?
Three elements:
the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element.
These three things are to be directly known.
Which three things are to be realized?
The three true insights.
Knowledge of the recollection of past lives is true knowledge; knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is true knowledge; knowledge of the destruction of the taints is true knowledge.
These three things are to be realized.
Thus these thirty things are real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise, and have been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
4. Four Things. Four things are very helpful; four things are to be developed; ... [as before] ... four things are to be realized.
What are the four things that are very helpful?
There are four wheels:
dwelling in a suitable locality, reliance on superior persons, right self-direction, and merit performed in the past.
These four things are very helpful.
Which four things are to be developed?
The four foundations of mindfulness.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
These four things are to be developed.
Which four things are to be fully understood?
The four nutriments.
Edible food, whether gross or subtle, is the first; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth.
These four things are to be fully understood.
What are the four things to be abandoned?
There are four floods:
the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
These four things are to be abandoned.
Which four things partake of decline?
The four yokes:
the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
These four things pertain to decline.
What are the four things that pertain to distinction?
The four dissociations:
The dissociation from the bond of sensual desire, the dissociation from the bond of existence, the dissociation from the bond of views, and the dissociation from the bond of ignorance.
These four things pertain to distinction.
What four things are difficult to penetrate?
There are four kinds of concentration:
concentration partaking of decline, concentration partaking of stagnation, concentration partaking of distinction, and concentration partaking of penetration.
These four things are difficult to penetrate.
Which four things are to be developed?
Four kinds of knowledge:
knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of inference, knowledge of the other’s mind, and knowledge of conventional designation.
These four things are to be brought forth.
Which four things are to be directly known?
The four noble truths.
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—
these four things are to be directly known.
What four things are to be realized?
The four fruits of asceticism—
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship.
These four states are to be realized.
Thus these forty-four things are real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise; they have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
5. Five Things:
Five things are of great service … [as before] … five things are to be realized.
Which five things are of great benefit?
The five factors of striving:
here, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He is free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive system that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and conducive to striving.
He is not fraudulent, not deceitful, and reveals himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.
These five qualities are very helpful.
Which five things are to be developed?
Five-factored right concentration:
pervasion by rapture, pervasion by pleasure, pervasion by the mind, pervasion by light, and the sign for reflection.
These five things are to be developed.
Which five things are to be fully understood?
The five aggregates of clinging.

The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
These five things are to be fully understood.
Which five things are to be abandoned?
The five hindrances:
the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
These five states are to be abandoned.
Which five things pertain to decline?
Five kinds of mental barrenness:
here, friends, a bhikkhu is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the Teacher.
Friends, when a bhikkhu doubts, wavers, is not convinced, and does not have confidence in the Teacher, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When the mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving—
this is the first wilderness of the mind.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is doubtful and uncertain about the Dhamma …pe… he is doubtful and uncertain about the Saṅgha …pe… he is doubtful and uncertain about the training …pe…
He is angry with his fellow celibate practitioners, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring ill will. Friend,
for that bhikkhu who is angry with his fellow celibate practitioners, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring ill will, his mind does not incline toward ardor,
devotion, perseverance, and striving.
That whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving—
this is the fifth wilderness of the mind.
These five things partake of decline.
Which five things partake of distinction?
The five faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
These five things pertain to distinction.
What five things are difficult to penetrate?
The five elements of escape.
"Here, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to sensual pleasures, his mind does not leap up at them, does not find confidence in them, does not settle upon them, and is not liberated from them.
But when he attends to renunciation, his mind leaps up at renunciation, finds confidence in it, settles upon it, and is liberated from it.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from sensual pleasures."
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by sensual pleasures—he is freed from them. He does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to ill will, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not become confident in it, does not settle in it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to non-ill will, his mind leaps forward into non-ill will, becomes serene, settles, and is liberated.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from ill will.
Whatever taints, distresses, and fevers arise conditioned by ill will—from those he is freed. He does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from ill will.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to cruelty, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle in it, and is not liberated by it.
But when he attends to non-cruelty, his mind leaps forward toward it, finds confidence in it, settles in it, and is liberated by it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from cruelty.
Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by cruelty—those he has escaped. He does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from cruelty.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to forms, his mind does not leap forward toward them, does not become settled, does not find stability, and is not liberated.
But when he attends to the formless, his mind leaps forward toward the formless, becomes settled, finds stability, and is liberated.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from forms.
And whatever taints, distresses, and fevers arise conditioned by form—from those he is freed. He does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from forms.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to personal existence (sakkāya), his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to the cessation of identity, his mind leaps forward into the cessation of identity, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and is liberated in it.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-cultivated, well-emerged, well-liberated, and dissociated from identity.
And those taints, distresses, and fevers that arise with identity as their condition—those he has escaped. He does not experience that feeling.
This has been declared as the escape from personal existence (*sakkāya*).
These five things are difficult to penetrate.
What five things are to be brought forth?
Right concentration possessing five kinds of knowledge:
the knowledge arises within oneself that "this concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future";
the knowledge arises within oneself that "this concentration is noble and spiritual."
The knowledge arises within oneself: "This concentration is not practiced by base men.
The knowledge arises within oneself: "This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained through tranquility, attained to unification, and is not forced or restrained by volitional effort.
The knowledge arises within oneself: "I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully."
These five things are to be brought forth.
Which five things are to be directly known?
The five bases of liberation—
In this case, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or some venerable companion in the holy life does so.
In whatever way the Teacher or that venerable companion in the holy life teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, in just that way he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.

In one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises; in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; and for one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the first basis for liberation.

Furthermore, friends, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does some other venerable companion in the holy life; yet he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard and mastered it.

In whatever way, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it, in that very way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.

As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises; for one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he feels pleasure; and for one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated.
This is the second basis for liberation.
Furthermore, friends, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does another venerable companion in the holy life do so;
nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and mastered it.
Nevertheless, he recites the Dhamma in detail by way of oral rehearsal as he has heard it and mastered it.

In whatever way, friends, a bhikkhu recites in detail the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it, in that very way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma in that Dhamma.

As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises; for one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he feels pleasure; and for one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the third basis for liberation.
Furthermore, friends, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does another venerable companion in the holy life do so;
nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it,
nor does he recite it in detail as he has heard and mastered it.
Moreover, he reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.
To whatever extent, friends, a bhikkhu reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered,
to that same extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning within that Dhamma.
And he experiences the Dhamma.

As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises; in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he feels happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the fourth basis for liberation.
Furthermore, friends, it may be that neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does some other venerable companion in the holy life;
nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it,
nor does he recite it in detail as he has heard and mastered it, nor does he [recite it] as he has heard...
He mentally reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been learned;
moreover, he has properly grasped, attended to, well retained, and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom some sign of concentration.
In whatever way, friends, that sign of concentration has been properly grasped and well attended to by the bhikkhu...
When that [teaching] is well-remembered and well-penetrated by wisdom in such and such a way, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.
In him who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises;

in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
This is the fifth basis for liberation.
These five things are to be directly known.
Which five things are to be realized?
There are five aggregates of Dhamma:
the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These five things are to be realized.
Thus these fifty states—real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise—are rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
6. Six States:
Six states are of great benefit... [and so on] ...six states are to be realized.
Which six things are very helpful?
The six principles of cordiality.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu maintains bodily conduct imbued with loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to inclusion, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu’s loving verbal action … [as above] … leads to unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu’s loving mental action … [as above] … leads to unity.

Furthermore, friends, whatever gains are righteous and righteously acquired—even if only as much as is contained in a single alms-bowl—a bhikkhu shares such gains with his virtuous companions in the holy life, enjoying them in common without making private hoards.
This too is a principle that is consoling... [as before] ...it leads to a state of unity.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells both in public and in private possessing those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating,
praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration;
this too is a quality that calls for recollection.
... [as before] ... it leads to unity.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells both openly and in private with his fellow brahmacārins, possessing that noble view which is emancipating and leads its practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering—that is, having attained such a view through the state of a recluse—this too is a principle that is consoling, endearing, and inspiring;
it leads to integration, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
These six things are very helpful.
Which six things are to be developed?
The six subjects of recollection:
Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities.
These six things are to be developed.
Which six things are to be fully understood?
There are six internal sense bases:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
These six phenomena are to be fully understood.
Which six things are to be abandoned?
The six classes of craving:
craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
These six things are to be abandoned.
Which six things partake of decline?
The six kinds of disrespect—
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher; [the same applies to] the Dhamma... the Saṅgha... the training... heedfulness... and hospitality.
These six things lead to decline.
What are the six things that lead to distinction?"
Six respects:
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells respectful and deferential toward the Teacher; [toward] the Dhamma …pe… the Saṅgha … the training … heedfulness … hospitality.
These six things partake of distinction.
Which six things are difficult to penetrate?
The six elements of escape.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:
‘Indeed, my liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken;
yet still, ill will persists, seizing hold of my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable One! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.’

"It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen that when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, ill will would still persist, taking possession of the mind—such a thing is not possible.
For this, friend, is the escape from ill will: namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness."
"Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:
‘Indeed, I have developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the liberation of mind through compassion;
yet still, cruelty persists, obsessing my mind.’"
To him it should be said: “Do not say so; do not speak thus, Venerable One; do not misrepresent the Blessed One...
For this, friend, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion.
But here, friend, a bhikkhu might say this:
‘Indeed, I have developed the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy … yet discontent still persists, seizing hold of my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not speak thus, Venerable Sir; do not say so …’ [and so on].
"For this, friends, is the escape from aversion, namely, the liberation of the mind through altruistic joy.
Then, friends, a bhikkhu might say here:
"The liberation of the mind through equanimity has been developed by me... [as before]..."
‘And yet passion still persists, having overwhelmed my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not speak thus, Venerable Sir; do not speak thus... [as before] ...
For this, friend, is the escape from passion, namely, the liberation of the mind through equanimity.’”
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say this:
“I have indeed developed the signless liberation of mind,
yet my consciousness still follows after signs.”
To him it should be said: “Do not say so, Venerable; do not speak thus to the Venerable one…” [as before] “…For this, friend, is the escape from all signs, namely, the signless liberation of mind.
Furthermore, friends, here a bhikkhu might say:
‘The thought “I am” has indeed vanished for me; I do not regard anything as “this I am”;
yet the arrow of doubt and perplexity still remains, obsessing my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable One! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.’

"It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen that for one who has eliminated the thought 'I am' and does not regard 'this I am,' the arrow of doubt and perplexity will remain obsessing the mind—such a thing is not possible.
For this, friend, is the escape from the arrow of doubt and perplexity: namely, the uprooting of the conceit 'I am.'"
These six things are difficult to penetrate.
What six things are to be produced?
The six constant abidings.
In this case, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
These six things are to be developed.
Which six things are to be directly known?
The six unsurpassed qualities:
The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection.
These six things are to be directly known.
What six things are to be realized?
The six direct knowledges:
Here, friends, a bhikkhu wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he passes through walls, enclosures, and mountains as if through space... [and so forth].
He moves without clinging, just as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water;
he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth; he travels cross-legged through the air like a winged bird;
and with his hand, he touches and strokes these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic.
He grasps and strokes [the earth] with his body, exercising mastery over it as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near.
He understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with his own.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" …pe… he understands an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say, one birth …pe… thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

…pe… Through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he abides therein.
These six things are to be realized.
Thus these sixty qualities are real, true, such, not otherwise, and not different; they have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
7. Seven Qualities:
Seven qualities are of great benefit … [as before] … seven qualities are to be realized.
Which seven things are very helpful?
The seven noble treasures:
the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom.
These seven things are very helpful.
Which seven things are to be developed?
The seven factors of enlightenment:

The mindfulness enlightenment factor, the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, the energy enlightenment factor, the rapture enlightenment factor, the tranquility enlightenment factor, the concentration enlightenment factor, and the equanimity enlightenment factor.
These seven things are to be developed.
Which seven things are to be fully understood?
There are seven stations of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first station of consciousness.
“There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first reappeared there.
This is the second station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods.”
This is the third station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.
This is the fourth station of consciousness.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form... [as before] ...having attained the base of infinite space, thinking "space is infinite," are reborn in the base of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, having attained the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "consciousness is infinite," are reborn in the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
These seven things are to be fully understood.
Which seven things are to be abandoned?
The seven underlying tendencies:

The underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
These seven things are to be abandoned.
Which seven things partake of decline?
Seven things that are contrary to the true Dhamma:
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is devoid of faith, he is shameless, he is unafraid of wrongdoing, he is of little learning, he is lazy, he is muddle-minded, and he is lacking in wisdom.
These seven things lead to decline.
Which seven things are conducive to distinction?
Seven true qualities:
here, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, he has a sense of shame, he has moral dread, he is learned, he is energetic, he is established in mindfulness, and he is wise.
These seven qualities pertain to distinction.
What seven qualities are difficult to penetrate?
The seven qualities of a true person.
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is one who knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows the proper measure, knows the right time, knows the assembly, and knows individuals.
These seven things are difficult to penetrate.
What are the seven things that should be developed?"
Seven perceptions:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
These seven things are to be developed.
Which seven things are to be directly known?
The seven bases for commendation:
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has intense desire for undertaking the training, and he does not lose his affection for undertaking the training in the future.
He has a keen desire for settling in the Dhamma, and his love for settling in the Dhamma remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for the removal of longing, and his love for the removal of longing remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for seclusion, and his love for seclusion remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for the arousal of energy and an undiminished love for the arousal of energy in the future.
He has a keen desire for mindfulness and discernment and an undiminished love for mindfulness and discernment in the future.
He has a keen desire for the penetration of views and an undiminished love for the penetration of views in the future.
These seven things are to be directly known.
Which seven things are to be realized?
The seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed.
"Here, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena have been clearly seen as they really are with correct wisdom as impermanent. And this, friends—
that for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed all conditioned phenomena have been clearly seen as they really are with correct wisdom as impermanent—
is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by relying upon which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed..."
A bhikkhu claims the destruction of the taints: “The taints are destroyed in me.
Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as similar to a pit of glowing coals.
And whatever... [as before] ...“The taints are destroyed in me.”

Furthermore, friends, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed slants toward seclusion, inclines toward seclusion, tends toward seclusion; it is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and has completely transcended all things that are the basis for the taints.
To this extent, friends... "My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, friends, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.
"Furthermore, friends... 'My taints are exhausted.
Moreover, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, the five faculties have been developed, well-developed. Furthermore, friends...
'My taints are exhausted.'"
Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and well developed.
Insofar as... [as before] ...he knows: "My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the noble eightfold path has been developed and well developed.
Furthermore, friends, when the noble eightfold path has been developed and well cultivated by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed,
this too is a power of that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims:
"My taints are destroyed."
These seven things are to be realized.
Thus these seventy things—real, true, such, not otherwise, not different—are rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
The first recitation section is finished.
8. Eight Things.
Eight things are very helpful … [as before] … eight things are to be realized.
What are the eight things that are very helpful?

There are eight causes and eight conditions that lead to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
What are the eight?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon the Teacher or upon a certain venerable companion in the holy life, in whom he has established a keen sense of shame and moral dread, as well as affection and reverence.

This is the first cause, the first condition, which leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.

Furthermore, he dwells in dependence upon a teacher or some venerable companion in the holy life, toward whom a keen sense of shame and dread of blame, as well as affection and reverence, are established. From time to time, he...
Having approached, he questions and interrogates:
"Venerable sir, what is this?
What is the meaning of this?"
Those venerable ones reveal to you what has not yet been revealed, clarify what has not yet been made clear, and dispel doubt regarding various matters that give rise to uncertainty.

This is the second cause, the second condition, for the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of that which has already been acquired.
Having heard that Dhamma, one should practice it with a twofold seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind.

This is the third cause, the third condition, which leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

This is the fourth cause, the fourth condition, which leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is learned, one who has retained what he has heard, and one who has accumulated what he has heard.
Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which are entirely complete and perfectly pure—
They praise the holy life; such teachings as these have been heard much by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well penetrated through right view.

This is the fifth cause, the fifth condition, which leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states.

This is the sixth cause, the sixth condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recalls what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.

This is the seventh cause, the seventh condition, which leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:
‘Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form;
such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling;
such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception.’
‘Such are volitional formations, such is the origin of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.

This is the eighth cause, the eighth condition that leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
These eight qualities are very helpful.
What eight qualities are to be developed?
The Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—
these eight things are to be developed.
Which eight things are to be fully understood?
The eight worldly conditions:
gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
These eight things are to be fully understood.
Which eight things are to be abandoned?
The eight wrongnesses:
wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
These eight things are to be abandoned.
Which eight things partake of decline?
The eight bases of indolence.
In this case, friends, a monk has work to do.
It occurs to him:
"I have work to do, and while doing the work my body will become weary; come now, I shall lie down."
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the first ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a monk has performed some work.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed performed work; while performing that work, my body is weary. Come now, let me lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy... [as before] ...
This is the second ground for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu must travel along a road,
and it occurs to him:
‘I must travel along a road, and as I travel along that road my body will become weary; what if I were to lie down?
He lies down and does not arouse energy...
This is the third ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has traveled along a road.
It occurs to him:
"I have indeed traveled along a road; while traveling along the road, my body is weary. Come now, I shall lie down."
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy...
this is the fourth basis for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain as much coarse or refined food as he requires for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:

"While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction; therefore, my body is weary and unfit for work. Come now, I shall lie down.
... This is the fifth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he obtains as much of coarse or refined food as he requires for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:
“While walking for alms in a village or town, I have indeed obtained as much of coarse or refined food as I required.”
‘I have eaten as much as I needed for full satisfaction; my body is heavy and unwieldy, as if it were smeared with fat.
Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down...
This is the sixth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a slight ailment arises in a bhikkhu, and it occurs to him:
“This slight ailment has arisen in me; there is reason to lie down. Let me lie down.
He lies down... [as before]...
This is the seventh ground for laziness.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recently recovered from an illness.
It occurs to him:
‘I have indeed recently recovered from an illness;
my body is weak and unfit for work, so let me lie down.
He lies down... [as before]...
This is the eighth ground for indolence.
These eight things pertain to decline.
What eight things pertain to distinction?
Eight grounds for undertaking work.
Here, friends, a monk has work to be done, and it occurs to him:
"Work indeed must be done by me; however, while doing that work, it is not easy to attend upon the Buddhas..."
‘I shall attend to the teaching; come now, I will arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the actualization of the unactualized.
Thus he arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the actualization of the unactualized.
This is the first basis for undertaking.
Furthermore, friends, a deed has been done by a bhikkhu,
and it occurs to him:
‘I have indeed performed work, but while performing that work, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas; let me now arouse energy.
… This is the second basis for arousing energy.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu must travel along a road.
It occurs to him:
"I must travel along a road, and while traveling along that road, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas; well then, let me arouse energy...
This is the third basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has traveled along a road.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed traveled along a road; while traveling along that road, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, let me arouse energy …” [and so on].
This is the fourth ground for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, while a bhikkhu is walking for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain as much coarse or refined food as he requires for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:
‘While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction; therefore, my body is light and fit for work.
Come now, let me arouse energy. … This is the fifth basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or town, obtains as much coarse or refined food as he requires for his full satisfaction.
It occurs to him:
“While wandering for alms in a village or town, I have obtained as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction.
My body is strong and fit for work; come now, let me arouse energy….”
This is the sixth basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a slight illness arises in a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
‘This slight affliction has arisen in me; however, it is possible that this affliction might increase. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the seventh basis for exertion.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recovered from illness, having not long risen from his sickness.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed recovered from illness; it has not been long since I arose from my sickness. It is possible that this affliction might recur.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached.”
‘For the attainment of what has not been attained, for the reaching of what has not been reached, for the realization of what has not been realized.
He arouses energy for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the reaching of what has not been reached, for the realization of what has not been realized.
This is the eighth basis for exertion.
These eight qualities pertain to distinction.
What are the eight qualities that are difficult to penetrate?
They are the eight inopportune moments, the eight unsuitable times for living the holy life.

"Here, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha; and the Dhamma is taught—leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Sugata.
Yet this person has been reborn in hell.
This is the first inopportune moment, the unfavorable occasion for living the holy life."

Furthermore, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha; and the Dhamma is being taught—leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata.
Yet this person has been reborn in the animal realm.
This is the second inopportune moment, the second unfavorable occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore...
[as before] ...one is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
This is the third inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore...
[as before] ...he is reborn in a certain class of long-lived deities.
This is the fourth inopportune and untimely moment for living the holy life.
Furthermore, ...
he is reborn in a border region among foreigners who are ignorant, where there is no access for monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen.
This is the fifth inopportune moment, the unfavorable time for living the holy life.
Furthermore...
this person is reborn in the central provinces, yet he holds wrong view and possesses perverted vision:
"There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done."
‘There is no result of kamma; there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world by their own direct knowledge and can make it known to others.’”
This is the sixth inopportune moment, the non-season for living the holy life.
Furthermore, ... [as before] ...
this person is reborn in the central provinces, yet he is dull-witted, stupid, and mute, not being capable of discerning the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This is the seventh inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore, ... [as before] ...
this person is reborn in the Middle Countries; he is wise, not dull-witted, nor deaf-mute, and is capable of discerning the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This is the eighth inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
These eight things are difficult to penetrate.
What eight things are to be brought forth?
The eight thoughts of a great person:
This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desire.
This Dhamma is for one who is contented, not for one who is discontented.
This Dhamma is for one who lives in seclusion; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in company.
This Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy; this Dhamma is not for one who is lazy.
This Dhamma is for one whose mindfulness is established; this Dhamma is not for one who is muddled in mindfulness.
"This Dhamma is for one who is concentrated; this Dhamma is not for one who is unconcentrated.
This Dhamma is for one possessed of wisdom; this Dhamma is not for one of poor wisdom.
This Dhamma is for one free from conceptual proliferation; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in conceptual proliferation. These are the eight qualities that should be brought forth.
Which eight things are to be directly known?
The eight bases of mastery:
one percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful or ugly, [thinking], "Having mastered them, I know and see them."
He perceives thus.
This is the first base of mastery.
Internally perceiving forms, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one knows and sees: "I know and see."
He perceives thus.
This is the second base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly, [thinking]: "Having mastered them, I know and see them."
He perceives thus.
This is the third base of mastery.
Internally perceiving no forms, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful and ugly; having mastered them, one knows and sees: “I know and see.”
He perceives thus.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Internally perceiving the formless, one sees external forms that are blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, and blue-luminous.
Just as an umā flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;

or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, might be blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster—even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster. Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see."
This is the fifth base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Just as, for example, a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster; just so—
Or else, just as there might be a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster;

even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster. Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as, for example, a *bandhujīvaka* flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster;
or just as, for example, a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Red in appearance, red in luster;

even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are red, red-colored, red in appearance, and red in luster, and having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Just as, for example, the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster;
or just as, for example, Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.

In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are white, of white color, white in appearance, and white in luster; having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).
These eight things are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*).
Which eight things are to be realized?
The eight liberations:
possessing form, one sees forms.
This is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally;
this is the second liberation.
He is intent only upon the beautiful.
This is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation.
Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the eighth liberation.
These eight things are to be realized.
Thus, these eighty things are real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise; they have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated;
with a concentrated mind, one knows and sees things as they truly are; knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted;
through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated.
These nine things are very helpful.
Which nine things are to be developed?
The nine factors of exertion for complete purification:
Purification of virtue is a factor of exertion for complete purity; purification of mind is a factor of exertion for complete purity; purification of view is a factor of exertion for complete purity;
purification by overcoming doubt is a factor of exertion for complete purity; purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path is a factor of exertion for complete purity;
purification by knowledge and vision of the way is a factor of exertion for complete purity; purification by knowledge and vision.
The factor of striving for complete purity, the factor of striving for purity of wisdom, and the factor of striving for purity of liberation.
These nine things are to be developed.
Which nine things are to be fully understood?
The nine abodes of beings:
There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first abode of beings.
"There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who were first reborn there.
This is the second abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods."
This is the third abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.
This is the fourth abode of beings.
"There are, friends, beings who are non-percipient and devoid of experience, such as the non-percipient deities.
This is the fifth abode of beings.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] 'space is infinite,' have reached the sphere of infinite space."
This is the sixth abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the seventh abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the eighth abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the ninth abode of beings.
These nine things are to be fully understood.
Which nine things are to be abandoned?
Nine states rooted in craving: dependent on craving comes seeking;
dependent on seeking comes gain; dependent on gain comes decision-making;
dependent on decision-making comes desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust comes attachment; dependent on attachment... [comes clinging].
Possession; dependent on possession, stinginess; dependent on stinginess, guarding;
and on account of guarding, there arise the taking up of sticks and weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech—many evil, unwholesome states come to be.
These nine things are to be abandoned.
Which nine things partake of diminution?
The nine grounds for resentment:
one harbors resentment thinking, "He has done me harm."
One harbors resentment, thinking, "He has done me harm";
one harbors resentment, thinking, "He will do me harm";
one harbors resentment, thinking, "He has done harm to someone dear and pleasing to me" ... [and so on] ...
‘He has acted for my harm,’ one harbors resentment... ‘He will act for my harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He has acted for the benefit of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me,’ one harbors resentment... [and so on].
“He is acting for my benefit”—thus one binds up resentment...
“He will act for my benefit”—thus one binds up resentment.
These nine things pertain to decline.
Which nine things partake of distinction?
Nine ways of removing resentment:
“He has done me harm; what can be done about it?”—thus one removes resentment.
‘He has acted for my harm; how could that be?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He will act for my harm; how could that be?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me... [and so on].
‘He has acted for my harm... he will act for my harm’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He has acted for the benefit of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me... [and so on].
“He has acted for my benefit...
he will act for my benefit—how could this be otherwise? In this way, one dispels resentment.
These nine qualities lead to distinction.
What are the nine things that are difficult to penetrate?
Nine diversities:
depending on the diversity of elements, there arises the diversity of contact; depending on the diversity of contact, there arises...
The diversity of feelings; dependent on the diversity of feelings, there arises the diversity of perceptions;
dependent on the diversity of perceptions, there arises the diversity of intentions; dependent on the diversity of intentions, there arises the diversity of desires;
dependent on the diversity of desires, there arises the diversity of fevers; dependent on the diversity of fevers, there arises the diversity of quests.
Dependent on diversity in search, there arises diversity in gain. ...
These nine things are difficult to penetrate.
What nine things are to be developed?
Nine perceptions:

the perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion.
These nine things are to be developed.
Which nine things are to be directly known?
The nine successive dwellings:

Here, friends, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
With the fading away of rapture, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna...
With the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form... [he] enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
These nine things are to be directly known.
Which nine things are to be realized?
The nine successive cessations:
for one who has attained the first jhāna, the perception of sensual desire has ceased.
For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought have ceased;
for one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased;
for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, inhalation and exhalation have ceased.
For one who has attained the base of infinite space, perception of form has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, perception of the base of infinite space has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, perception of the base of infinite consciousness has ceased.
For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased;
for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, both perception and feeling have ceased.
These nine things are to be realized.
Thus these ninety dhammas are real, true, such, not otherwise, and have been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
10. Ten Dhammas:
Ten dhammas are of great benefit... [as before] ...ten dhammas are to be realized.
Which ten things are very helpful?
The ten qualities that make one a protector:

Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is virtuous ... [as above] ... he trains in the rules of training.
This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is learned ... [as above] ... his view is well-penetrated.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu is learned … [as before] … this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Again, friends, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who associates with good people...
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is easy to correct and possesses the qualities that make him easy to correct; he is patient and receives instruction respectfully.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu [is endowed with] ... [and] instruction—this too is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is skillful and diligent regarding those various minor duties for his fellow celibates; he possesses the discernment of the proper means therein, being capable of acting and capable of organizing.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu ... [as before] ... this too is sufficient for providing support.
This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is one who loves the Dhamma, delights in its proclamation, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu... [as before] ...is filled with sublime joy.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu … [as before] … this too is a quality that provides a protector. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the cultivation of wholesome states. … [as before] … This too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu ... [as before] ...
this too is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was said long ago. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu ... [as before] ...
this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu...
[as before] ...this too is a quality that provides a protector.
These ten qualities are very helpful.
Which ten states are to be developed?
The ten kasiṇa bases:
one perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable.
One perceives the water-kasina … one perceives the fire-kasina … one perceives the air-kasina.
One person perceives the blue kasiṇa… one person perceives the yellow kasiṇa… one person perceives the red kasiṇa…
One person perceives the white kasiṇa;
another perceives the space kasiṇa;
another perceives the consciousness kasiṇa—above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable.
These ten things are to be developed.
Which ten things are to be fully understood?
The ten bases:
The eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, and the tangible-object-base.
These ten phenomena are to be fully understood.
Which ten phenomena are to be abandoned?
The ten wrong states:
wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation.
These ten things are to be abandoned.
What are the ten things that partake of decline?
They are the ten courses of unwholesome action:
killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
These ten things pertain to decline.
Which ten things pertain to distinction?
The ten courses of wholesome action.
Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct,
abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, non-covetousness,
non-ill will, and right view.
These ten things partake of distinction.
What are the ten things that are difficult to penetrate?
The ten abodes of the noble ones.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, is possessed of six factors, has a single guard, has four supports,
has shaken off individual dogmatic views, has thoroughly relinquished seeking, has untroubled intentions, has tranquilized bodily formations,
and is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has abandoned five factors?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned ill will, has abandoned sloth and torpor, has abandoned restlessness and remorse, and has abandoned doubt.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one who has abandoned five factors.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu endowed with six factors?
Here, friends, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with six factors.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu guarded by a single guard?
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu is possessed of a mind guarded by mindfulness.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has a single guard.
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have the four supports?"
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures another; having reflected, he avoids another; having reflected, he dispels another.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has the four supports.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has shaken off individual speculative tenets?"

"Here, friends, whatever various individual truths there are among the many ordinary recluses and brahmins, all of those have been shaken off, driven out, abandoned, vomited up, released, relinquished, and discarded by that bhikkhu.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has shaken off individual truths.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has utterly renounced seeking?"
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures, has abandoned the search for existence, and has stilled the search for the holy life.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has completely relinquished his searches.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose intentions are undisturbed?"
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned thoughts of sensual desire, abandoned thoughts of ill will, and abandoned thoughts of cruelty.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one whose intentions are undisturbed.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose bodily formations are tranquil?"

"Here, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has tranquilized bodily formations.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in mind?"
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one whose mind is well-liberated.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose wisdom is well-liberated?"
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu understands: "Lust has been abandoned by me; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising in the future. He understands:
"Hatred has been abandoned by me...
[and so on] ...incapable of arising in the future."
‘Delusion has been abandoned by me...
[and so on] ...it is of a nature not to arise again in the future,’ he understands.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
These ten things are difficult to penetrate.
What ten things are to be generated?
Ten perceptions—

The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
These ten states are to be developed.
What ten states are to be directly known?
The ten bases for the wearing away [of kamma]:
For one of right view, wrong view is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are also worn away for such a person.
For one of right intention, wrong intention...
for one of right speech, wrong speech...
for one of right action, wrong action... [is abandoned].
Wrong livelihood for one of right livelihood;
wrong effort for one of right effort;
wrong mindfulness for one of right mindfulness.
For one of right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away;
for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away;
for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is worn away.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by wrong liberation—these have been worn away by him.
These ten things are to be directly known.
What ten things are to be realized?

The ten qualities of one beyond training: the right view of one beyond training, the right intention of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training,
the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, and the right concentration of one beyond training.
“...the knowledge of one beyond training, and the liberation of one beyond training.
These ten things are to be realized.
Thus these hundred things—real, true, such, not unreal, not otherwise—are rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.”
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta.
The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words.
The *Dasuttara-sutta*, the eleventh, is finished.
The Pāṭhika Chapter is finished.

The wheel-turning monarch, the foremost of all;
the palace of serene confidence,
and the marks of a Great Man.
The Siṅgālāḷa, the Āṭānāṭiya,
the Saṅgīti, and the Dasuttara—
by means of these eleven suttas,
It is called the Pāṭhika-vagga.
